Foreign-Supported Sabotage Hits Aerospace & Defense Sites Across Northern Italy

Milan – A coordinated series of sabotage incidents attributed by Italian authorities to foreign state actors has severely disrupted operations at multiple Aerospace & Defense industry sites in northern Italy. The ongoing situation, which began early Tuesday, has prompted heightened security protocols, partial evacuations, and production stoppages at several facilities owned by leading sector firms.

According to the National Aerospace Security Bureau, at least six manufacturing plants and research centers in Lombardy and Piedmont have experienced targeted disruptions. These include unauthorized access, tampering with sensitive equipment, and deliberate damage to production lines. The sites affected belong to companies such as Aerotecnica Novara, Difesa Sistemi Italia, and AeroVeneto S.p.A. No casualties have been reported, but industry unions say hundreds of workers have been sent home as a precaution, with many more operating under restricted conditions.

“This is a grave and unprecedented attack on our national capabilities,” said Marcello Bianchi, president of the Italian Aerospace & Defense Association. “The precision and timing of these incidents strongly suggest external orchestration by hostile interests. We are working closely with law enforcement and intelligence agencies to restore operational safety and resume normal activity.”

At the Aerotecnica Novara facility in Vercelli, staff described confusion and concern as alarms sounded and emergency procedures were enacted. “We heard the alert just after the morning shift started,” said one technician, who asked not to be named. “Supervisors told us to stop work and leave the assembly area immediately. Everyone is worried about what will happen next.”

Industry analysts warn that the ongoing disruptions could have long-term consequences for Italy’s Aerospace & Defense sector, which employs over 50,000 workers nationwide. “Even short-term stoppages can set back complex production schedules by weeks or months,” said defense industry analyst Giulia Ferretti. “If these attacks continue, the financial and strategic impact could be substantial, especially for firms with international commitments.”

Union leaders have called for enhanced security measures and greater transparency from management. “Our priority is the safety of the workforce,” said Roberto Leone of the Federazione Lavoratori Metalmeccanici. “We demand that companies keep workers fully informed and provide assurances that sites will not reopen until all risks have been addressed.”

As investigations continue, security has been stepped up at all major Aerospace & Defense industry sites in the region. Authorities have not disclosed details about the suspected foreign involvement but have stated that all available resources are being deployed to safeguard critical industry operations.
